TIP 10: Adverse event under-reporting at Caldera Pharmaceuticals
CHANNEL: secure drop
RECEIVED: 05 May 2026

I am a pharmacovigilance specialist at Caldera Pharmaceuticals, which markets an approved oncology biologic under the brand name SAVENTRA (rinatumab) for adult patients with relapsed B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. I have been at Caldera since 2021 and on the SAVENTRA safety team since the drug's approval in late 2022.

I am reporting a pattern of adverse-event under-reporting in the post-marketing safety surveillance for SAVENTRA. The pattern is straightforward: a category of patient-reported adverse experiences is being routed away from formal safety case processing, which means those experiences are not being included in periodic safety updates submitted to FDA or in the global safety database used to support label updates.

SAVENTRA is distributed through a single specialty pharmacy network, and patients who experience side effects often call into Caldera's patient assistance program (PAP) before they tell their oncologist. The PAP call center, which sits inside Caldera's commercial organization, is supposed to triage these calls under a documented procedure: any caller describing a medical experience suggestive of an adverse event is supposed to be warm-transferred to pharmacovigilance and a case opened.

In approximately Q3 2024, the PAP call routing rules were modified to add a "patient inquiry — symptom resolution" disposition. Calls dispositioned this way are not transferred to PV. They are routed back to the call center supervisor, who provides general counseling and closes the call. There is no PV record created. The audit trail of the call is retained in the commercial CRM, not in the safety database.

I ran a query of PAP call records against PV cases for the period October 2024 through February 2026. In that window:

- 14,820 total PAP calls were received from SAVENTRA patients.
- 3,140 of those calls were dispositioned as "patient inquiry — symptom resolution."
- Of those 3,140, my keyword review of the call notes identified 612 calls that, in my judgment, described medical experiences that should have been opened as PV cases. The most common patterns were neutropenic fever (an important known risk for SAVENTRA), severe infusion-related reactions occurring at home post-infusion, and one cluster of approximately 40 cases describing acute neurologic symptoms that were not previously characterized in the drug's label.

The neurologic cluster is what concerns me most clinically. The pattern across those 40 calls — which I could compile with the descriptions in the call notes — is broadly similar in onset timing and described symptomatology. None of these calls resulted in a PV case being opened, and none are reflected in the PSUR submitted to FDA in March 2026.

I have raised this internally twice. I sent a written summary to our Head of Safety, Dr. Veronique Blas, in January 2026. I was told the call routing rules were "operationally appropriate" and that the responsibility for PV reporting rested with healthcare providers, not with PAP call dispositions. I escalated to our Compliance function in February. The response I received was that the matter had been reviewed and was closed.

I have retained: the call routing rules documentation, the CRM call records (de-identified pulls within my legitimate access), the PSUR submitted in March 2026, and the comparison spreadsheet I assembled. I am willing to be identified to FDA but not to the company until I have a formal protective order.

TIP 1: Cost-plus / fixed-price labor mischarging at Vermilion Defense
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 28 April 2026

I am writing about Vermilion Defense Systems, a tier-one prime contractor based in Tucson. I work as a Subcontracts Manager II on the Hawkeye-X airborne ISR program, an Air Force cost-plus-fixed-fee program that has been the prime focus of the Tucson site since 2022. I have been with Vermilion since 2020 and on Hawkeye-X since the program transitioned out of risk-reduction in late 2023.

The issue I am reporting is systematic mischarging of labor between two co-located programs. Hawkeye-X runs cost-plus. Vermilion has a separate Air Force program out of the same building, designated Granite IV, that is firm-fixed-price. The two programs share approximately 30 percent of their engineering staff and the entire RF integration lab.

Beginning in March 2024, labor hours that I can document as having been worked on Granite IV tasks began appearing in the Hawkeye-X cost reports under indirect engineering categories. The clearest evidence is the engineering labor burn on Hawkeye-X, which jumped 17.8 percent month-over-month in March 2024 with no scope change, no staffing change on the Hawkeye-X charge numbers, and no corresponding increase in deliverable output.

I have copies of the monthly indirect rate detail reports for January 2024 through March 2025, the underlying subcontractor invoices showing original task allocation, and the revised allocation reports that follow what I believe is an internal reclassification process that did not go through documented program-control review. The reclassification entries are made under a single user account, "wcr-batch01," which does not correspond to a named program-control analyst on either program.

My estimate, based on the records I have, is that Vermilion has overbilled the Air Force by approximately $4.6 million on Hawkeye-X across calendar 2024 and Q1 2025. I cannot estimate Q2 2025 directly because I rotated to a new responsibility on 14 April 2025 and lost regular access to the Hawkeye-X cost reports, but my former colleague who is still on the program told me informally in November 2025 that "the pattern hasn't changed."

I have already retained personal counsel and have begun the process of preparing a formal disclosure under the False Claims Act. I am submitting this through your channel because I want the underlying pattern to be on a journalistic record as well, in case the qui tam process is slow or my identity is disclosed before any sealed complaint can be unsealed.

I am willing to share the indirect rate detail reports, the subcontractor invoices, the reclassification audit trail, and a written timeline. I would prefer not to be contacted at any Vermilion email address or through any Vermilion-affiliated communication channel.

TIP 2: Unallowable costs billed through indirect pool on Navy maintenance contract
CHANNEL: secure drop
RECEIVED: 02 May 2026

I am a senior cost accountant at Vermilion Defense Systems' Norfolk facility, which holds the cost-reimbursable maintenance and overhaul contract for two squadrons of Aegis destroyers, contract N00024-22-C-2188. I have worked at Vermilion since 2017 and in cost accounting since 2019.

What I am reporting is the routine treatment of expressly unallowable costs as allowable indirect expenses, which are then flowed through to the Navy via our negotiated indirect rates. Under FAR 31.205 a number of cost categories are unallowable on cost-reimbursement government work — the most relevant ones here are entertainment, lobbying, golf and country club memberships, executive air travel beyond the cost of commercial coach, and alcohol.

Beginning in fiscal year 2023 I started seeing expense reports run through the "Program Management — General" indirect cost pool that on review were clearly unallowable. Examples I can document:

- Two memberships at the Currituck Yacht Club, totaling $48,400 across 2023 and 2024, coded as "client relationship management."
- Twenty-three trips on a chartered Gulfstream operated by an entity called Bayfront Aviation, totaling roughly $612,000 across 2023 through Q1 2025, coded as "executive transportation - mission essential." The flight logs show several of these trips originated and terminated in non-program locations, including Aspen, Cabo San Lucas, and Hilton Head.
- Approximately $189,000 in 2024 and $94,000 through Q1 2025 in payments to a firm called Arden Strategies, which our public lobbying disclosures identify as a federal lobbying firm. The invoices were coded as "policy research and analysis."
- Roughly $73,000 in 2024 in event-bar charges from corporate dinners, coded as "training and meeting expenses."

The total of items I have personally identified as unallowable but billed allowable through the indirect pool is approximately $2.3 million across fiscal 2023 through Q1 fiscal 2025. The Aegis maintenance contract is the largest single absorber of indirect costs at our site, so the majority of this flowed to the Navy.

I raised this in writing to Vermilion's Director of Government Compliance, Wendell Truax, in two memoranda dated 11 September 2024 and 03 February 2025. I received an acknowledgment to the first and no response to the second. After the second memo I was removed from the indirect rate review committee and reassigned to a non-program accounting role.

I have retained the original GL extracts, the expense reports with imaged receipts, the T&E approval workflow records, and copies of both internal memoranda. I am willing to identify myself to a DCAA investigator under appropriate protections, but I would prefer initial contact be made by an attorney rather than by a journalist.

TIP 3: Subcontractor markup pass-through overcharging on Air Force ground systems contract
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 30 April 2026

I am a senior subcontract administrator at Vermilion Defense Systems' Colorado Springs site. I have worked at Vermilion since 2020. I am writing about a sustained pattern of overcharging the federal government on a cost-reimbursable Air Force ground systems contract through inflated subcontractor pass-through pricing.

The contract is FA8730-22-C-0019, a cost-plus-incentive-fee program for ground station hardware and integration in support of an unclassified Space Force mission. The contract has a substantial subcontracted content — approximately 42 percent of the total contract value passes through to about a dozen Tier-2 suppliers. Subcontractor costs are billed to the government on a pass-through basis, plus Vermilion's negotiated material handling rate of 6.8 percent.

What I have observed and can document is that beginning in approximately Q2 2023, the dollar amount Vermilion invoices to the government for subcontractor work has not matched the dollar amount Vermilion actually pays the subcontractors. Specifically, on five subcontracts that I have administrative responsibility for, the program is billing the government against subcontractor list prices while paying the subcontractor a negotiated discounted price under separately executed side-letter agreements that are not part of the prime-flowed subcontract.

The mechanism: the formal subcontract document references a "list price" tied to the subcontractor's standard rate sheet. The side letter, executed separately, applies a 14 to 22 percent discount in exchange for volume commitments and accelerated payment terms. The program bills the government using the subcontract list price, not the actual paid price.

For the five subcontracts I have visibility into, the pricing differential adds up as follows across calendar 2023 through Q1 2026:

- Subcontractor A (RF subassemblies): list-price billing $14.2M, actual paid $11.6M. Differential overbilled to government: $2.6M.
- Subcontractor B (precision machined parts): $8.4M billed, $7.1M paid. Differential: $1.3M.
- Subcontractor C (cable harnesses): $6.8M billed, $5.4M paid. Differential: $1.4M.
- Subcontractor D (test equipment): $4.1M billed, $3.6M paid. Differential: $0.5M.
- Subcontractor E (custom enclosures): $3.2M billed, $2.6M paid. Differential: $0.6M.

The total differential across just these five subcontracts is approximately $6.4M billed to the government against costs that Vermilion never incurred. This is the classic profile of a False Claims Act violation: invoices submitted at a price the contractor knows is higher than the price actually paid.

I raised the pricing differential in writing to my Director of Subcontracts, Ronan Westerly, in October 2024 and again in March 2025. The response in both cases was that the side-letter discounts were "commercial terms separate from the government cost record." I do not believe DCAA would accept that characterization on a cost-reimbursable contract.

I have retained: the formal subcontracts, the side-letter agreements, the supplier invoices showing actual payment amounts, and the customer invoices submitted to the government. I am willing to share these with DCAA or with a federal qui tam counsel.

TIP 4: Labor category mischarging on Army cost-plus cyber range task order
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 03 May 2026

This concerns Vermilion Defense Systems and a cost-plus-fixed-fee task order supporting cyber range operations at Aberdeen Proving Ground (W9113M-23-D-0041), issued under Vermilion's Army IDIQ vehicle. I am the project manager on the task order. I have been with Vermilion since 2022 and on this task order since its award in May 2023.

The mischarging I am reporting is in the labor category structure, which I believe is the simplest and most cleanly documented form of direct labor fraud on a cost-reimbursable contract. The task order has eight approved labor categories, each with a negotiated fully-burdened hourly billing rate ranging from $112/hr (Engineer I) to $284/hr (Senior Cyber Architect IV). The categories have minimum education and experience qualifications written into the task order.

What I have observed and can document is that approximately 60 percent of the work being billed under "Senior Systems Engineer III" ($218/hr) and "Senior Cyber Architect IV" ($284/hr) is actually being performed by employees who do not meet the contractual qualifications for those categories. In several cases the work is being performed by employees who were classified as "Engineer I" or "Engineer II" in our internal HR system at the time of the work.

I prepared a side-by-side comparison covering Q3 2024 through Q1 2026. For each invoice I matched the timecards against the employees' contemporaneous personnel records. The pattern:

- 14,600 hours billed at the SSE-III rate were performed by employees whose personnel record at the time showed Engineer I or Engineer II classification. At the rate differential between the categories, this represents approximately $1.41 million in over-billing.
- 4,200 hours billed at the SCA-IV rate were performed by employees whose record showed Senior Engineer or below. Differential overbilling: approximately $620,000.
- Total over-billing identified: approximately $2.03 million across the six quarters.

The mechanism, as I understand it, is that our Program Director Ariel Kessenbaum directs the back-office to assign labor categories at invoicing based on "what the customer needs filled" rather than the actual qualifications of the engineer performing the hours. The task order's contracting officer is not informed of this practice.

I raised this concern verbally to Kessenbaum on 17 January 2026 and was told that "the customer is happy with the deliverables and that's what matters." I raised it in writing to our Compliance Officer, Maren Vista, on 22 January and was told that the labor category review was "an internal HR matter."

I have retained: the approved labor category descriptions from the task order, exports from our timekeeping system showing employee-to-charge-code mappings, copies of submitted invoices, and the personnel records (mine to access as PM) showing the classifications at time of performance. I am willing to provide everything to an investigator under appropriate confidentiality.

TIP 5: Phantom travel and per-diem fraud at Vermilion Defense Systems
CHANNEL: secure drop
RECEIVED: 06 May 2026

I work as a senior travel coordinator at Vermilion Defense Systems, supporting Vermilion's services-side sites in Florida and Virginia. I have been in this role since 2018. I support travel for roughly 350 program employees who routinely travel to government customer sites.

I am reporting what I believe is a systematic pattern of fraudulent travel and per-diem claims that flow into our G&A and overhead pools and from there into the rates we bill the federal government on cost-reimbursable work. The pattern has three features.

First, phantom travelers. Beginning in mid-2023, I started seeing travel authorizations and corresponding expense reports submitted under the names of employees who, on cross-check against badge access and HR rosters, were not actually traveling on the dates claimed. The pattern concentrates around three names — two of which I now believe are dormant employee accounts retained from 2021 and 2022 separations, and one of which is the legal name of an executive's adult child who is not a Vermilion employee at all.

Second, duplicate claim submissions for the same trip. I have identified 37 trips between January 2024 and February 2026 where two distinct expense reports were filed against effectively the same itinerary — same origin, same destination, dates within one or two days of each other, both with hotel and per-diem claims. In 31 of the 37 cases, the two expense reports correspond to two different traveler names. In the remaining six the same traveler submitted twice.

Third, weekend and personal travel coded as program work. I cross-referenced 240 expense reports against badge access records at the customer sites being claimed as the destination. In 89 cases, the traveler had no badge swipes at the destination customer site during the claimed travel window. The most common pattern is a Friday-departure / Monday-return trip claimed against a customer-site engagement, where the actual flight log shows the destination city had no relationship to the program of record.

My estimated dollar exposure based on what I can directly tie to records I have:

- Phantom travelers: approximately $214,000 across 2024 and 2025.
- Duplicate claims: approximately $86,000 across the same period.
- Personal-trip coding: approximately $312,000.
- Total identified: approximately $612,000. I believe the actual figure across all programs and all years is materially larger.

The dollar amount per incident is small enough that no individual transaction triggers our finance team's threshold-based review. The cumulative exposure across cost-reimbursable contracts is what I am asking someone to look at.

I raised the duplicate-claim pattern to my supervisor, Inez Donato, in October 2024. She told me to "stop running unauthorized reports" and reminded me my role is to "facilitate travel, not audit it." I did not raise the personal-trip pattern internally because I did not believe it would be received any differently.

I have retained the underlying expense report exports, the badge access reports, and the flight log records I cross-referenced. I will not identify myself except to a federal investigator under written protection.

TIP 6: Cardiac adverse event recoding before NDA submission at Caldera Pharmaceuticals
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 27 April 2026

I am writing about Caldera Pharmaceuticals, a Boston-headquartered diversified pharmaceutical company. I work as a clinical data analyst on the Phase III pivotal program for vemorelibant, the company's lead candidate for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. The drug is currently under FDA review with a PDUFA action date in Q3 2026.

I am reporting that Caldera reclassified a cluster of cardiac adverse events from the Phase III pivotal trial before the NDA submission was finalized, in a way that I believe materially understates the drug's cardiac safety profile in the data presented to FDA.

In approximately February 2026, the Executive Risk Committee — which includes our CEO Anita Korhonen, CMO Dr. Felipe Salgado, and General Counsel Brian Westmore — directed the safety team to reclassify eleven cases that had originally been coded as "Grade 2 cardiac dysrhythmia, treatment-related" in the integrated safety database. After the reclassification, those eleven cases were coded as "Grade 1 dysrhythmia, treatment relationship indeterminate." The recoded dataset was the version submitted to FDA.

I attended the 06 February meeting where the reclassification was discussed. The discussion lasted approximately forty minutes. Dr. Salgado initially argued against reclassification on the grounds that the temporal pattern across the eleven cases — onset within 14 days of dose initiation in nine of eleven — was clinically suggestive of treatment relationship. He was overruled after Westmore raised concerns about labeling implications and commercial impact. Korhonen made the final call. Westmore subsequently drafted standardized rationale language that was inserted into the SAE narratives.

The clinical relevance of the recoding is that, at Grade 2 with attributed treatment relationship, the cluster would likely have triggered an FDA safety query and possibly a label warning around cardiac monitoring. At Grade 1 with indeterminate causality, the cluster falls below the threshold that would prompt either action.

I have access to both the pre-recoding and post-recoding database snapshots. The case-level coding changes are visible in the audit trail. I also have:

- The agenda and meeting calendar entry for the 06 February session.
- An email chain in which Westmore circulates the draft narrative language under the subject "revised SAE rationales — for biostat review."
- The pre-recoding version of the integrated safety summary table that was used in the December 2025 internal sign-off.
- The post-recoding version that was included in the NDA submission package.

I want to be clear about what I am and am not alleging. I am not, on the basis of these eleven cases alone, alleging that vemorelibant has unacceptable cardiac risk. I am alleging that the safety dataset Caldera submitted to FDA does not reflect the original investigator-reported coding, and that the recoding was driven by labeling and commercial considerations rather than by the medical adjudication process described in the protocol.

I am willing to share documents through a secure channel. I would prefer initial contact be with FDA OSI or with qui tam counsel rather than with the company.

TIP 7: Toxicology data exclusion before IND submission at Caldera Pharmaceuticals
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 01 May 2026

I am a research scientist in nonclinical pharmacology at Caldera Pharmaceuticals' Cambridge research site, working in the small molecule pipeline focused on inflammatory disease. I have been at Caldera since 2022. I am writing about how data from our 13-week rat tox study were handled in advance of the IND submission for our lead inflammation program, CAL-2104, an oral JAK1-selective inhibitor for moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis.

The pre-IND meeting with FDA was held in November 2025. The 13-week rat tox study (Study Number TOX-2104-013) was the pivotal study supporting the proposed clinical starting dose. The study ran four dose groups: vehicle, 3 mg/kg/day, 10 mg/kg/day, and 30 mg/kg/day. The clinical starting dose was set at a no-observed-adverse-effect-level (NOAEL) corresponding to the 10 mg/kg/day group.

What I observed and can document is that the original tox study report identified findings of hepatocellular hypertrophy and elevated ALT in the 10 mg/kg/day group at the week-13 sacrifice, in 7 of 12 animals in that cohort. These findings, if reported as treatment-related, would have moved the NOAEL down to the 3 mg/kg/day group and reduced the proposed clinical starting dose by approximately one-third.

Beginning in mid-September 2025, the program team — specifically the SVP of Development, Halford Brent, and our CMO, Dr. Marisol Yance — directed the toxicology lead to reclassify the 10 mg/kg findings as "background" rather than treatment-related. The rationale documented in the revised study report cited "high inter-animal variability in the strain" and pointed to two of the seven animals as having had pre-study elevated ALT values. The other five animals in the affected group had within-range pre-study values.

I attended a 24 September 2025 program meeting where Dr. Yance directly told the toxicology lead, Dr. Pranav Iyer, that the 10 mg group findings would be characterized in the briefing book as "non-adverse, monitored." Dr. Iyer pushed back on the call and was overruled. The IND-enabling briefing book sent to FDA on 02 October 2025 did not include the original 7-of-12 finding; it described the hepatic findings as "minimal, non-progressive hypertrophy without ALT elevation, considered non-adverse."

I retained: a copy of the original toxicology study report dated 18 August 2025, the revised report dated 25 September 2025, the briefing book draft circulated 30 September 2025, and meeting notes from the 24 September program meeting. I do not have audio of the meeting; my notes are contemporaneous.

I am asking that someone independent review whether the briefing book accurately characterized the 13-week rat findings. I am not, on my own, able to evaluate clinical risk at the proposed starting dose; what I can evaluate is whether the data were reported faithfully.

I am willing to share documents through a secure channel. I am still employed at Caldera and would prefer to remain anonymous in any initial reporting.

TIP 8: Stability test re-analysis on FDA-submitted ophthalmic generic
CHANNEL: intake form
RECEIVED: 29 April 2026

I work as a QC analyst at Caldera Pharmaceuticals' generics manufacturing operation, with sites in Cleveland and Mumbai. I am based at the Cleveland site. I have been with Caldera since 2020.

I am reporting practices in our QC stability program for product CP-OS-061, an ophthalmic preserved-solution generic for which Caldera filed an ANDA in March 2025 and received tentative approval in February 2026. The product is currently anticipating final approval and launch.

The issue concerns the 12-month stability timepoint testing. Stability protocols require that finished product samples be stored under defined conditions and tested at protocol-defined timepoints (3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24 months) against pre-defined acceptance criteria for assay, related substances (impurities), pH, preservative content, and visual appearance. The data are submitted to FDA in support of the proposed shelf life and storage conditions.

For CP-OS-061, the 12-month long-term timepoint samples were tested in the second week of November 2025. The original test results showed two related substances exceeding the qualified specification — Impurity-B at 0.18 percent against a 0.15 percent specification, and Impurity-D at 0.31 percent against a 0.25 percent specification. The original LIMS records show these out-of-specification (OOS) results were entered on 14 November 2025 by analyst K. Senthilnathan.

What happened next is outside the OOS investigation framework that the protocol requires. Rather than initiate a Phase I lab investigation under our SOP-QC-101, our QC Manager Jeevan Aravind directed that the samples be re-tested using HPLC method M-OS-061-B, an alternate method that had been validated as a qualifier rather than a release method. The alternate method is less sensitive in the 0.1-0.3 percent impurity range. The re-test under M-061-B returned results within specification (Impurity-B at 0.12 percent, Impurity-D at 0.22 percent).

The official record submitted to FDA shows only the M-061-B results, marked as the result of record. The original M-061-A results are present in the LIMS audit trail but were not included in the stability annual update submitted to the agency in February 2026.

I have screenshots of the LIMS audit trail showing both the original entry and the subsequent record-of-record reassignment, the chromatograms from both test methods, the M-061-B method validation report (which characterizes it as a qualifier method, not a release-equivalent method), and Aravind's email of 17 November 2025 instructing the re-test.

I have not raised this internally beyond a single conversation with my immediate supervisor in November 2025, who told me the matter had been "handled by QA management." Caldera's senior QA leadership reports up through the same chain as Aravind, and I do not have confidence that an internal escalation will be received differently than my initial conversation.

I would prefer initial contact be with FDA OSI rather than the company. I am willing to provide all the documentation I have retained.

TIP 9: Bioequivalence study site data manipulation at Indian study site
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 04 May 2026

I am a clinical research associate at Ardent Clinical Research, a contract research organization headquartered in New Jersey with global monitoring operations. I am writing about a bioequivalence study sponsored by Caldera Pharmaceuticals' generics division for an extended-release antihypertensive product the sponsor intends to file as an ANDA.

The study (Protocol BE-CP-2024-09) is a single-dose, two-period, two-treatment crossover bioequivalence study comparing Caldera's test formulation to the reference listed drug. The study was conducted at a single clinical pharmacology site, Bharadwaj Clinical Research Centre in Pune, between June and September 2025. I have monitored studies at Bharadwaj on three prior occasions across 2022 through 2024.

What I observed during my on-site monitoring visit in October 2025 raised concerns that I am reporting now because I do not believe my CRO management has acted on what I escalated internally.

The first concern is the bioanalytical concentration data. The plasma concentration-time curves from the test treatment, when plotted in aggregate, show an unusually clean adherence to the modeled dose-response curve, with within-subject variability lower than what I have observed in any previous bioequivalence study at this or any other site. The within-subject coefficient of variation for AUC was reported at 4.8 percent. Typical bioequivalence studies for extended-release products show within-subject CV in the 12 to 22 percent range.

The second concern is the eDiary timestamp pattern. Subjects in the study were required to log meal completion, water intake, and ambulation events in an eDiary application during the in-clinic confinement periods. On review of the eDiary export, I identified that across the 36 subjects, on five separate occasions during Period 1 confinement, 14 to 19 subjects' eDiaries logged the same event type within a 90-second window. The clustering pattern is consistent with the diaries being completed by a single staff member rather than by individual subjects.

The third concern is the chain-of-custody on the bioanalytical samples. The shipment manifest shows the samples leaving Bharadwaj on 22 September 2025 in a temperature-controlled shipper. The sponsor's bioanalytical lab, Coastal Bioanalytics in Hyderabad, logged receipt on 23 September. The temperature recorder file pulled from the shipper, however, shows a 41-minute period during transit when the recorder was not active. The site coordinator, Dr. R. Vasudev, told me on the audit visit that the recorder had been "briefly turned off for battery management."

I escalated all three issues to my line manager, Director of Clinical Operations Mira Halton, in a 14 October 2025 written report and again verbally on 28 October. I was told the issues were "noted" and that the sponsor would be informed. The study is now being prepared for ANDA submission. To my knowledge no formal data integrity investigation has been opened.

I have retained: the bioanalytical data exports, the eDiary timestamp file, the temperature recorder export, my monitoring report, my email correspondence with Halton, and the sponsor's response to my queries.

I am at the mid-career level professionally and would prefer not to be identified except to FDA OSI investigators directly.
